I'm reporting a dangerous gas-leak problem with our KitchenAid 48-inch dual-fuel range, Model KFDC558JSS, which runs on liquid propane and is installed in our home kitchen. It has six gas burners, each with a front knob that controls the gas and the igniter. One of the six burners is defective. When that burner is turned on, the gas flows continuously but the igniter never sparks, so it just pours out raw, unlit propane and does not stop. On a normal burner the gas only comes out when it is actually lighting. On this one that is broken, so the gas keeps running with no flame. It does not take a hard turn either. The knob can get bumped on, but the real danger is that once gas is flowing, it never ignites and never shuts off on its own. This is not a fluke. It happens every time, it is easy to reproduce, and it has happened multiple times. The escaping propane builds up fast and fills the house. If we did not catch it by smell, say it happened overnight while we were asleep, or when no one was in the kitchen, the home could fill with gas and any spark, such as a light switch, the AC kicking on, or the refrigerator, could set off a fire or explosion. This has already gotten bad enough that I had to get my wife and young kids out of the house until it cleared because I was afraid it would blow. The worst case here is that my whole family could be killed in an explosion or poisoned in their sleep. We only use the range for normal cooking. We are not doing anything wrong with it. This happens during ordinary use. KitchenAid and Whirlpool sent their service people out and they saw it themselves. Two different KitchenAid service contractors watched me reproduce the problem and agreed it was happening. They fixed the valve and igniter on one burner that was doing this, but then refused to fix a second burner that does the exact same thing, and now they are telling me that a burner leaking gas into our home is not a defect. Letter to AO Smith: I purchased an AO Smith 50 gallon propane water heater in April, 2014. Since that time I have had a recurring problem with the water heater overheating. Initially the problem was diagnosed as a faulty gas control valve, but after 3 valve replacements it became obvious that was not the case. Fast forward to today and I find myself at an impasse with your technical support department. I live in [REDACTED] and have a second home about 1.5 hours away that I visit 3-4 days a week. During the time I am away it has become apparent that turning down the temperature setting on the heater does not prevent temperatures of 150-160 degrees (a potential risk of scalding) being exhibited when I return. [REDACTED], the head of your technical support, has told me that the pilot light alone is causing the excessive heating and the only solution is for me to shutdown the heater when I leave and relight it when I return. In my opinion this is a ridiculous solution to the problem. The inability to keep the heater in a nominal temperature range with the proposed solution would result in tremendous inconvenience on a weekly basis, and potential impairment of the heater's functionality (igniter wearing out and excessive repeated temperature changes). This condition indicates to me that the heater does not have proper temperature control.

I have one of the A. O. Smith recalled water heaters (Model Number 153.330290, Serial Number 1144T450775). The water heater burner and controller were replaced via the CPSC recall process (CPSC Recall Number 19-029) on April 21, 2020. In early November 2020, the water heater burner started to make a loud humming noise 10 seconds after the burner is ignited and lasts 2 seconds. In early December 2020, it also started to make a second much louder humming sound after another 25 seconds that lasts 10 seconds. I would not have expected a new burner to have this problem. Either the burner is defective or the installation was not correctly done. This is a serious issue because the burner is vibrating (humming) when it is heating, and it could eventually physically tear and cause a fire. I send an e-mail to Ashland City Support (help@hotwater.com) who had originally provided the list of plumbers to perform the recall. They responded that this is not their problem and to contact Sears at 888-287-9322. Although the burner assembly was part of the recall, they claim that “Only the gas control valve was part of the recall, we replaced the burner assembly as a courtesy.” Per the Consumer Product Safety Commission recall notice, "The water heater's gas burner screen develops tears. The water heater's burner can then create excess radiant heat, posing a fire hazard if the water heater is installed directly on a wood or other combustible floor." Thus, the burner assembly was part of the recall and not a “courtesy.” Claiming that it was a “courtesy” is a fraud. The telephone number that they provided for Sears is a non-working number that is always busy. After further e-mail exchanges, they said to contact Sears at 800-469-4663. I have also called the telephone number for Sears (866-880-4661) on the CPSC recall notice, but I have not had any success in speaking to someone about the recall. I am always transferred to a non-working number. Sears had also failed in the recall process.
